analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave insurance program funded by a small payroll tax.
analysis.headline: The FAMILY Act drew 37 Senate cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, but never received a committee hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a national paid family and medical leave insurance program run by a new office inside the Social Security Administration. A worker who needed leave for a new child, a serious illness of their own, or care for a family member could receive two-thirds of their pay, capped at $4,000 a month, for up to 60 caregiving days. It would be funded by a 0.2% payroll tax on both employees and employers, and a 0.4% tax on self-employment income, paid into a dedicated trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people who need leave but have no paid leave at work. Today, whether a new parent or a worker facing cancer treatment gets paid time off depends almost entirely on the employer; lower-wage workers are the least likely to have any. The bill would cover employees who qualify for Social Security disability insurance and had earnings in the prior year, plus self-employed people, who currently have no employer to provide leave at all. It also protects applicants from being fired or penalized for using the benefit, with a private right to sue for back pay and attorney's fees [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid family or medical leave

how_it_helps.text: Gives covered workers up to 60 days of partial pay per benefit year: two-thirds of wages, at least $580 and at most $4,000 per month, for any of the family and medical reasons already recognized under the Family and Medical Leave Act, including birth, adoption, the worker's own serious health condition, and care for a spouse, parent, child, or domestic partner.
Covers self-employed people, who currently have no way to get paid leave, with a 0.4% self-employment tax buying the same benefit, and includes special rules so railroad employees are covered too.

Makes it unlawful to fire or discriminate against a worker for applying for or using the benefit, and lets the worker sue in federal or state court for lost wages, liquidated damages, and attorney's fees, with the Social Security Commissioner also able to enforce in court.
Sets a floor without overriding better arrangements: state paid leave programs are not preempted, and nothing in the bill weakens a union contract or employer plan that provides more generous leave.

Funds the whole program with a dedicated trust fund from a 0.2% payroll tax split evenly between employees and employers, plus a 0.4% tax on self-employment income, rather than from general borrowing or from the Social Security trust funds, which the bill expressly protects.

analysis.who_pays: Every employee pays 0.2% of wages (about $2 per $1,000 earned) and every employer pays a matching 0.2%, whether or not they ever take leave; self-employed people pay 0.4% of their net earnings. The tax starts 120 days after enactment and applications open 18 months later, with an initial Treasury appropriation for startup costs that must be repaid within 10 years [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: All workers and employers via payroll tax

drawbacks.text: The tax falls on everyone from day one, including workers and small businesses that never take or grant leave, so some people pay in for years and get nothing back.

Benefits are modest and tightly capped: a five-day waiting period is unpaid, benefits stop after 60 caregiving days in a benefit period, and the $4,000 monthly cap means higher earners get a smaller share of their usual pay replaced.
Low-wage part-time workers get the $580 monthly minimum, which is a real but small cushion, and the benefit is reduced for anyone also collecting unemployment or workers' compensation.

A good-faith objection from employers is that a new mandatory payroll tax adds cost per employee at the same time as the bill's anti-retaliation rules create litigation exposure for any company that mishandles a leave request.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a small, permanent tax on every wage dollar for a benefit most workers will need at some point, and that a large share of workers, especially low-wage ones, currently have no access to. The cost is broad but shallow, about $2 per $1,000 of wages from each side. The design weaknesses are real: 60 days is shorter than what several state programs offer, the unpaid waiting period falls hardest on people living paycheck to paycheck, and the tax begins before any benefit can be claimed. On balance the bill delivers a large, concrete benefit to ordinary workers for a modest, evenly spread cost, and its main flaw is stinginess, not design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the bill on February 4, 2021, with 37 cosponsors including Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and both Senate independents, Bernie Sanders and Angus King.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, which holds jurisdiction over Social Security and payroll taxes.
No further action of any kind was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress.
The bill died on January 3, 2023, when the 117th Congress ended and all unpassed bills expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and higher-earning workers who would have paid the new payroll tax without expecting to use the benefit are better off because the bill never moved. Workers without paid leave at their jobs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoiding the new payroll tax

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 37 cosponsors was a Democrat or independent and not a single Republican signed on; the bill never got far enough for a roll-call vote.

industries.note: The bill imposes a 0.2% payroll tax on every employer for every dollar of wages, and makes paid leave a federal entitlement rather than a perk each employer controls. That is a small cost per worker, but it ends employer discretion over whether leave is paid and who qualifies.

They would pay a 0.4% tax on self-employment income but gain access to paid leave benefits that no employer currently provides them, so the trade runs in their favor and alongside the public interest in coverage.
